tier_reason: Upgraded C to A for the popcount and set-algebra rows: benchmark code is public (benchmark.cpp, run as 'benchmark -p -r 10000' with Linux perf counters against popcount_scalar_naive_nosimd and *_scalar_naive_nosimd), the compiler (gcc 8.2.1 20180905) and CPU (Core i3-8121U Cannon Lake) are stated in the README, and the flags come from the public CMakeLists.txt (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release, CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS -std=c++11, so CMake's GCC Release default -O3 -DNDEBUG; kernels picked at run time via target attributes, so no -march is needed). The README's pospopcnt table is not produced by this repo's benchmark: it is copied unchanged from mklarqvist/positional-popcount.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Popcount: 16.4x at 1024 64-bit words, 21x at 8192, 4.2x at 1048576 (1.0x at 4 words); set-algebra cardinality (AND/OR/XOR): 15.3x at 1024 word pairs, 13.7x at 8192, 2.8x at 1048576, 0.8x at 4; all in CPU cycles per 64-bit word versus an 8-bit lookup-table scalar loop compiled with vectorization disabled. The README also shows a positional-popcount table (up to 138.71x at 65536 values for pospopcnt_u16_avx512_harvey_seal), but those numbers are identical to the mklarqvist/positional-popcount README (measured there with gcc 7.3.1) and are not produced by libalgebra's benchmark.cpp.
corrections.baseline: naive scalar code with auto-vectorization disabled (__attribute__((optimize("no-tree-vectorize")))): popcount_scalar_naive_nosimd and intersect/union/diff_scalar_naive_nosimd, which count bits with an 8-bit lookup table (STORM_popcnt_lookup8bit), not the POPCNT instruction
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 8.2.1 20180905 (Red Hat 8.2.1-3) per README; CMakeLists.txt forces CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release and sets CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS to -std=c++11 (CMake's GCC Release default adds -O3 -DNDEBUG); no -march flag, the SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX512BW kernels use __attribute__((target(...))) with CPUID dispatch; run as 'benchmark -p -r 10000'
corrections.caveats: Baseline is a deliberately naive 8-bit lookup-table loop with vectorization disabled (about 8.1 cycles per 64-bit word for popcount, 5.0 for set algebra), not the POPCNT instruction or __builtin_popcountll, so the speedups overstate the gain over a tuned scalar loop. The positional-popcount table in the README is copied from mklarqvist/positional-popcount (same numbers, measured there with gcc 7.3.1); libalgebra's benchmark.cpp does not benchmark pospopcnt. The library packages kernels from positional-popcount and the Lemire/Kurz/Mula AVX2 popcount work (sse-popcount), so it overlaps with those entries. Release build defines NDEBUG, so the assert(a == b) correctness check in the perf popcount path is compiled out and the set-algebra path has no check. Single machine; data freshly generated each iteration and cache-resident (README calls it a practical upper limit). No commits since 2019-12-16.

notes: Numbers on the README match the record exactly. Upgraded to A because CMakeLists.txt pins the build (Release, -std=c++11) and benchmark.cpp runs the named naive baselines; the record wrongly said no build file existed. The pospopcnt claim belongs to positional-popcount (batch-10), so the orchestrator may want libalgebra listed on its popcount and set-algebra rows only, or folded as a near-duplicate; the weak lookup-table baseline should be recorded as a shortcoming.

tier_reason: First-party: the README quotes rebar rank output from benchmarks/record/x86_64/2023-08-26.csv, and both memchr and rebar are by the same author. Benchmark code and engine build commands are public (benchmarks/engines.toml, cargo build --release), but no CPU model or RUSTFLAGS are stated anywhere I opened, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (2023-08-26 record, memchr 2.5.0 vs Rust std 1.73.0-nightly): geometric mean of speed ratios 1.03 vs 6.50 prebuilt (std about 6.3x slower) and 1.04 vs 5.26 oneshot (about 5.1x), derived from page data. Newest record benchmarks/record/x86_64/2026-07-30.csv (memchr 2.8.3 vs Rust std 1.99.0-nightly 1a833e165), pairwise geometric mean of median times: 4.64x prebuilt and 3.93x oneshot over 53 memmem benchmarks; 2.02x vs glibc memmem (libc/memmem/oneshot, 54 benchmarks, libc faster on 8); single-byte memchr 1.10x vs glibc memchr (15 benchmarks); StringZilla 5.0.5 memmem beats memchr on 39 of 54 benchmarks (memchr takes about 1.6x StringZilla's time, geometric mean) (all derived from page data).
corrections.baseline: Rust standard library substring search (rust/std/memmem: str::find / str::matches); the same rebar records also run glibc memmem and memchr through the libc engine (libc/memmem/oneshot, libc/memchr/oneshot)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Engines built with 'cargo build --release' (benchmarks/engines.toml); Rust std baseline 1.73.0-nightly 180dffba1 in the 2023-08-26 record and 1.99.0-nightly 1a833e165 in the 2026-07-30 record; libc engine version recorded as 'unknown'; RUSTFLAGS, target-cpu and the rustc version for the memchr engine not stated
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1.6k stars; about 1.54 billion crates.io downloads (crates.io API, 2026-10-11)
corrections.caveats: Baseline is Rust's std, not a C or C++ library; the README comparison covers substring search (memmem) only, and its numbers come from the 2023-08-26 record although newer records exist (2025-09-25, 2026-07-30). In the newest record the std gap is smaller (about 3.9x to 4.6x), the win over glibc memmem is about 2x, single-byte memchr is roughly at parity with glibc memchr (glibc 1.06x faster in the 2023 record, memchr 1.10x faster in 2026), and StringZilla, already catalogued in wave 1, is faster on 39 of 54 memmem benchmarks. The std prebuilt engine cannot exclude searcher construction, which the README admits. No CPU model or RUSTFLAGS stated. Author wrote both the library and the rebar harness. It is a Rust crate (C++ use needs FFI) and a string-search library rather than a general SIMD intrinsics library.

notes: README numbers match the record; I derived extra ratios from the public CSVs (pairwise geometric means of median times). Main shortcomings to record: first-party, no hardware stated, std-only headline, glibc memchr parity, StringZilla faster in memchr's own 2026 record; category fit is weak (string search rather than SIMD intrinsics library).

tier_reason: First-party CSVs from public benchmark code (benchmark/benchmark_main_v3.cpp) with flags in CMakeLists.txt, but no CPU model or compiler stated, so C. The tier stays C, but the claim is overstated: the 18.7x headline comes from dot-product rows whose scalar reference is handicapped (volatile locals on every element, noinline, and optnone under Clang).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Against plain non-vectorized scalar loops (simd_v3_benchmark_results_fixed.csv): Jaccard up to 7.57x, Hamming up to 4.64x, L2 up to 2.04x, cosine up to 2.03x, SAXPY up to 1.69x. Dot-product rows (the 18.7x headline: F32 at 8192 elements, 18.67x in simd_v3_benchmark_results_1751127313.csv; 16.73x peak in the fixed CSV) are measured against scalar_dot_*_no_autovec references that load each element into volatile locals, so they do not show a gain over normal scalar code. In the third CSV (simd_v3_benchmark_results.csv), F32 dot product runs at 0.18x to 1.84x of scalar (one 4.64x outlier at 1537), and 38 of 175 rows are slower than scalar. Memory-bandwidth, KNN, batch-cosine and edge-case rows report a placeholder 1.0.
corrections.baseline: the benchmark's own scalar reference loops: scalar_dot_product_no_autovec / scalar_dot_{f16,i8,bf16}_no_autovec for dot products (volatile per-element loads, noinline, optnone under Clang), plain inline scalar loops for L2, cosine, Hamming, Jaccard and SAXPY; the whole benchmark target is built with auto-vectorization disabled
corrections.compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt Release benchmark targets: -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -mavx2 (plus -mavx512f -mavx512bw -mavx512vl when supported), and with SIMD_DISABLE_AUTO_VECTORIZATION ON (the default) also -fno-tree-vectorize -fno-slp-vectorize -fno-tree-loop-vectorize and DISABLE_SCALAR_AUTOVEC (which adds a GCC optimize pragma or '#pragma clang optimize off' over the benchmark functions); compiler and version used for the CSVs not stated
corrections.caveats: Headline 18.7x is not a valid gain over scalar code: the dot-product scalar references copy every element into volatile locals (forced stack store and reload), are noinline, and become optnone (-O0 equivalent) under Clang, while the whole benchmark target is built with auto-vectorization disabled. The third CSV in the repo, probably from before the scalar reference was changed (code comments say 'FIXED: Scalar reference with auto-vectorization DISABLED'), shows F32 dot product at 0.18x to 1.84x of scalar and 38 of 175 rows slower than scalar. The fair-looking rows (plain scalar loops without auto-vectorization) give 1.7x to 7.6x. No CPU model or compiler stated (CSV lists AVX512F, FMA, F16C, VNNI); three CSVs with different results and no record of which run is current; vectors of 15 to 16384 elements, cache-resident. Tiny repo (2 stars, 2 commits on 2025-06-28); no comparison with Highway, xsimd or Eigen. README mentions AMD enterprise support, but the repo is a personal project.

notes: Downgrade for an overstated claim, kept at C on the non-dot kernels; shortcoming to record: the 18.7x headline is measured against a volatile-handicapped scalar dot product (optnone under Clang), and an earlier CSV in the same repo shows the F32 dot product at 0.18x to 1.84x of scalar. If the orchestrator treats the headline as the entry's claim, the AssemblyScript crippled-baseline precedent (C to D) would apply.
